To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in patients receiving pharmacologic daily doses of prednison, calcium absorption is decreased and serum 25(OH) D is low.
calcium absorption was decreased in patients treated with daily high doses of corticosterone, but not in those treated with daily low doses or with high doses given in an alternate-day regimen.
in exogenous hyper-cortisonism intestinal calcium absorption was decreased, which was associated with a decrease in serum 25-hydoxyvitamin D.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of corticosterone on the absorption of calcium from the gastrointestinal tract.
the effect of corticoid treatment on intestinal calcium absorption.
the relationship between the dose of cortisone and intestinal calcium absorption in exogenously hypercortisonic patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the impairment of intestinal calcium absorption in exogenously hypercortisone patients is due to the decreased serum concentration of the biologically active form of vitamin D, 1, 25-dihydroxycalciferol, resulting from the inhibition of 1-hydroxylase activity in the renal cortex by the high circulating levels of the glucocorticoid hormone.

the administration of pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoid hormones to normal individuals results in a dose-related decrease in serum 25-OHD, a decrease in intestinal calcium absorption, and a decrease in serum ionized calcium, all of which are corrected by the administration of 0.4 mug of 1,25-(OH)2D3 per day.

in exogenous hyper-cortisonism intestinal calcium absorption is impaired in relation to the dose of cortisone administered, and that the impairment of calcium absorption is related to a decrease in the circulating levels of 25-OH-cholecalciferol, the prohormone of the vitamin D hormone, 1, 25-dihydroxycalciferol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of corticosterone on the intestinal calcium absorption is dose-related, and that it can be corrected by the administration of a physiological or near physiological dose of 1,25(OH)2D3.
the dose of cortisone is the major determinant of the effect of corticoids on calcium absorption.
corticosteroid-induced calcium malabsorption is due to an abnormality of vitamin d metabolism and not due to a direct effect on the intestine.
